messages.subject: R/qtl marker/population size limits re: linkage mapping
messages.subject_clean: R/qtl marker/population size limits re: linkage mapping
messages.body_plain:
Karl:

I have been using R/qtl for genetic map construction for some time now, but do not know if there are marker number and population size limits in using R/qtl commands for this purpose.

My colleagues and I have a soybean population of 1500 F5-derived RILs obtained from a biparental mating of homozygous parents (G. max x G. soja).  We would like to order about 2000 polymorphic SNP markers on each of the 20 soybean chromosomes, though we recognize that the extent of recombination available in this population will impose limits on marker ordering).  The soybean has a total (Kosambi) map length of about 2500 cM).

The purpose of this project is to help us deal with a few assembly sequence problems in the published soybean DNA sequence.

Can one use the R commands described in http://www.rqtl.org/tutorials/geneticmaps.pdf to handle this many markers and individuals?

We would welcome any suggestions you might offer with respect to computer specifications (memory, etc.) to handle this problem.

Thanks in advance for your reply.

- Jim

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] R/qtl marker/population size limits re: linkage mapping
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] R/qtl marker/population size limits re: linkage mapping
messages.body_plain:
There's no limit on the number of markers or individuals that can be handled within R/qtl.  Analyses are slower, and some plots become hard to read, but 1500 RILs at 2000 SNPs shouldn't pose a problem.

karl

messages.subject: converting genotypes from JoinMap to rQTL format
messages.subject_clean: converting genotypes from JoinMap to rQTL format
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am using a 4-four way phase-known outbred cross for QTL mapping. The
parents segregate heterogeneously such that all possible genotypic
classes are possible. My data is currently in JoinMap format. I am
trying to convert it to rQTL format.

Joinmap as the following coding scheme to represent this.
These are the possible segregation types for the cross parents:

ab x cd (fully informative)
ef x eg (3 alleles, 1 shared, both parents heterozygotes)
lm x ll (2 alleles, 1 homozygote, 1 heterozygote)
nn x np (2 alleles, 1 homozygote, 1 heterozygote, opposite parent)
hk x hk  (2 alleles, both heterozygotes)

Based on my understanding, the intercross coding options for rQTL are
thus:
ac = 1
bc = 2
ad =	3
bd = 4
A = AC or AD	5
B = BC or BD	6
C = AC or BC	7
D = AD or BD	8
AC or BD	 = 9
AD or BC	 = 10
not AC = 11
not BC = 12
not AD = 13
not BD = 14

I am trying to convert my data from Joinmap to rQTL. Here is what I
have come up with:

ab x cd = recode:
ac        = 1
bc        = 2
ad	    = 3
bd	    = 4

lm x ll
ll	= 5	AC or AD
ml	= 6	BC or BD

nn x np
nn	= 7	AC or BC
np	= 8	AD or BD

I am fairly certain the above is correct. I am less sure about the
following:

ef x eg	code as ab x cd?
ee	       = 1	ac
fe	       = 2	bc
eg	       = 3	ad
fg	       = 4	bd

hk x hk
hh	9	AC or BD	 or 10
hk	10	AD or BC	  or 9	?
kk	9	AC or BD	 or 10

I think the following are for 3:1 dominant markers:
not AC = 11   AD, BC, or BD
not BC = 12   AC, AD, or BD
not AD = 13   AC, BC, or BD
not BD = 14   AC, AD, or BC

Can anyone confirm I am doing this correctly? Or have any ideas on the
the last few segregation types?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: converting genotypes from JoinMap to rQTL format
messages.subject_clean: converting genotypes from JoinMap to rQTL format
messages.body_plain:
Ok, I think I figured it out (with the assistance of my lab
mates :-) ).   3+ heads are better than 1.

Yes, I can code the ef x eg type using 1,2,3,4 (ab x cd). Since I know
phase, I know the true history of the alleles.

I now realize I can combine the numbers, and they are not limited to
groups of different segregation types.

So, for hk x hk, the possible kids are hh, hk, kk
This translates into ac, bc or bd, ad.
hh = ac = 1
hk = ad or bc  = 10
kk = bd = 4

(genotype 9 would be used if the parents are hk x kh, for example)

For dominant 3:1 type markers (e.g. AFLPs), we can use a combination
of 11,12,13 or 14, AND one of the others.
So for example, say we have a dominant marker F with alleles F and f
(F dominant to f) and our parents are Ff x Ff, we would see two types
of kids:
F_ and ff in a 3:1 ratio. This translates in to F_ = 14 (not ff, i.e.
not BD in our coding scheme) and 4 (ff = BD).

I still welcome any thoughts or insights that confirm all this.

Genetics is fun.
Thanks!
